home.hero.eyebrow: Senior Product Manager · Digital products specialist
home.hero.lead:
I'm a designer, a product manager and a mom.
Those three things are what made me good at finding and solving problems.
home.sobre.p1: I started out in graphic design in 2009, moved into digital in 2014, spent four years running my own business in the creative economy, and have worked in digital products since 2020. For the last five years I have been in product and leadership roles, keeping the roadmap close to the business through the scale-up from a 60-person startup to a 350-person company with R$ 392 million in revenue in 2025. (@vaideturbi 💙)
home.sobre.p2: In product, what I do best today is structuring badly defined problems, the pains nobody quite owns, and turning them into a hypothesis, a validation and a result. I am strong in continuous discovery and research, strategy and roadmap, impact-driven prioritization, experimentation, product analytics, business metrics, and generative AI applied to the journey and to operations.
home.sobre.p3: Coming from design keeps me from thinking about form, the solution, before I understand function very well, the pain and the goal. It also gives me richer tools for practicing empathy and holding on to the customer's point of view.
home.traj.6.d: I created a cross-functional customer journey practice to bring the customer's pains together in one place and put the customer's voice into the culture and into how the teams see their work.
home.traj.5.d: I took over the Growth and Experience portfolio, with revenue, retention and cost targets under my responsibility for the first time.
home.traj.4.d: The only product person across three squads and the lead of a nine-person team, running the backlog through a phase of aggressive growth.
home.traj.3.d: I led the UX and technology fronts on digital transformation and innovation projects, from banking to e-commerce.
home.traj.2.d: I founded and ran a creative hub built on collaborative projects, supporting culture and education through creative economy events.
home.traj.1.r: From art assistant to creative director
home.traj.1.d: Seven years in advertising, branding and digital media, working for brands such as Toyota, Samsung, TIM, Meta and ANBIMA.
home.case1.titulo: Customer Journey: creating the practice and strengthening a client first culture
home.case1.desc: The invitation to create an area that would look after the customer journey came with a pain already in the open: the experience metrics were falling and none of the problems had an owner.
home.case2.titulo: Chatbot self-service: changing the invoice due date
home.case2.desc: One of the main reasons subscribers reached out was needing to move the due date, to avoid a failed charge and the friction that came with it.
home.case3.titulo: Flexible subscription: from MVP to proving the value proposition
home.case3.desc: Three years of experimenting, validating and expanding, from the first demand test to the product being fully defined.
case.assinatura.capa.sub: from MVP to proving the value proposition
case.assinatura.tldr.contexto:
Turbi has rented cars on demand, by the hour and by the day, since 2017.

In 2022, the pain holding back the growth of the business was the lack of revenue predictability and an occupancy that reset to zero every month.
case.assinatura.tldr.acao: We built the subscription product step by step, validating a completely new line of business, mapping the gaps in the market and positioning the product with a clear differentiator and a defined value proposition.
case.assinatura.tldr.resultado: Today the subscription carries most of the fleet's utilization, with thousands of active contracts.
case.assinatura.contexto.titulo: Car subscription already existed, just not the Turbi way.
case.assinatura.contexto.p1: The market sold subscriptions through consultants, with rigid contracts and a car chosen by category months in advance. Turbi had the opposite in its DNA: you sign up on your own in the app, you get a specific car, and there is no counter to go to.
case.assinatura.contexto.p2: For the business, the bet was revenue predictability and better fleet utilization during the week. For the customer, it was having a car to call your own without the bureaucracy of owning one. The challenge was time to market running against a complete discovery, for a new audience with a different reason to use the car.
case.assinatura.quote1.t: Having a new car, simple and immediate, without the bureaucracy of buying or renting, and knowing I will not be left stranded.
case.assinatura.quote1.a: The value proposition as customers described it in research
case.assinatura.discovery.metodo: With a clear picture of what the business needed in order to launch, we validated the demand and scaled the product in less than a year.
case.assinatura.ct1.d: A page selling our 30-day rental as a new way of using a car, to measure demand before there was a product.
case.assinatura.ct2.d: Now inside the app, anyone booking a car for more than 15 days was offered the subscription. Selling inside a flow that already existed was the cheapest way to test price and duration.
case.assinatura.ct3.t: First version with a sign-up flow of its own
case.assinatura.ct3.d: The subscription stopped depending on a booking and became a front door of its own. That is when the product finally had a base worth analyzing.
case.assinatura.ct4.d: An analysis of the subscriber base, conversations with subscribers and leads, a quantitative survey, a study of mileage use and a benchmark. Out of that came the rules, the flow, the prototype and the usability test.
case.assinatura.ct5.d: Terms from 1 to 12 months with a progressive discount, choice of the specific car, recurring billing, renewal and upgrades within the contract.
case.assinatura.ct6.t: Structured V2: mileage allowances and additional driver
case.assinatura.ct6.d: The rolling mileage allowance tiers shipped together with a free additional driver, plus the alert for going over the allowance.
case.assinatura.ct7.d: Revisiting the flow and the copy, evolving the product through journey mapping, with questions answered inside the product instead of in support.
case.assinatura.achado1.t: Service had to be more human than we assumed
case.assinatura.achado1.d: Turbi's value proposition is self-service, but discovery showed that customers needed to talk to someone in this flow, because of the price point and the longer contract.
case.assinatura.achado2.t: Handing the car over fast was our biggest differentiator
case.assinatura.achado2.d: No competitor delivered in under 7 days, and when a carmaker was involved the wait reached 60. Driving away with the car the same day was the advantage our base mentioned most in the survey.
case.assinatura.achado3.t: The car not being brand new was the obstacle to overcome
case.assinatura.achado3.d: Car subscription was a synonym for a brand new car, and our fleet may already have been on the road. Getting past that came down to transparency, with the full details of the car visible before signing.
case.assinatura.decisoes.label: The product decisions
case.assinatura.feat1.t: From 1 to 12 months, with a progressive discount
case.assinatura.feat1.d: Nothing like it existed at the time: subscriptions on the market started at 12 months.
case.assinatura.feat3.d: Whatever you do not drive in one month carries over to the next, within the contract.
case.assinatura.feat4.t: Automatic renewal, managed in the app
case.assinatura.feat4.d: The customer sees when the contract ends and decides to renew or close it without talking to anyone.
case.assinatura.feat5.d: Term, category or mileage allowance, without having to close the contract and sign a new one.
case.assinatura.feat6.d: Up to 5 people drive the same car at no extra cost.
case.assinatura.feat7.t: No deposit and no fuel included trade-off
case.assinatura.feat7.d: No competitor dropped the security deposit, and keeping ours could have blocked conversion. Fuel was left out on purpose.

case.assinatura.resultado.titulo: The value proposition proved itself and scaled
case.assinatura.res1.l: growth in subscriptions, from the first test version to the consolidated one
case.assinatura.res2.l: active contracts today, in a product that started life as a landing page
case.assinatura.res3.l: months of contract length, when subscriptions on the market started at 12
case.assinatura.resultado.fecho2: The 2022 pain was revenue predictability and an occupancy that reset to zero every month. Today the subscription is the product that carries most of the fleet's utilization and gives the business that predictability.
case.venc.capa.sub: Changing the due date of the subscription invoice
case.venc.tldr.contexto: The subscription was always billed on the day the customer signed up, and there was no way for them to change that date on their own. It blocked sign-ups and drove a high volume of contacts to support.
case.venc.tldr.acao: We designed and shipped a self-service flow inside the pre-support chatbot, where the subscriber changes the due date without having to talk to anyone.
case.venc.tldr.resultado: Around 80% self-service retention in the first weeks, settling at about 75%, and the delivery worked as planned on the first deploy.
case.venc.contexto.titulo: The invoice due date was a recurring problem.
case.venc.contexto.p1: The due date was set from the day the customer signed up and froze there. Someone who signed up on the 28th paid on the 28th for the rest of the contract, even if their own cash flow ran on another calendar.
case.venc.contexto.p2: It looked like a small problem and was expensive in practice, because it touched recurring billing, risk, and the customer's relationship with a car they use every day and could have taken away by a failed payment.
case.venc.quote1.t: We make this change all day long, one at a time, with a basic flow that already exists in the back office.
case.venc.discovery.metodo: We set out to understand the problems in the subscription flow by analyzing the reasons for contact tied to paying this product's invoice. The discovery question was: out of everything that makes a subscriber talk to us about billing, what would they solve on their own if they could?
case.venc.ct1.d: We understood the customers' problems from the transcripts of the tickets categorized under this theme across the support channels.
case.venc.ct2.d: Before shipping the new flow, we had to solve structural problems in the chatbot tool that was already running in production.
case.venc.ct4.d: The productization work that set every rule and criterion of the feature, in a cross-functional forum with the areas involved.
case.venc.ct5.d: Defining the flow, the screens, the tone of voice and the user experience.
case.venc.ct6.d: Subscribers started solving it in pre-support, with simulation, editing and payment, without talking to an agent.
case.venc.ct7.d: Retention measured week by week until the number settled and we understood that the remaining overflow needed manual negotiation analysis.
case.venc.achados.titulo: Three findings that shaped the solution
case.venc.achado1.t: The risk was real and had to be part of the rule
case.venc.achado1.d: No date change could happen with an open balance. The customer had to settle the debt first, and that became an explicit condition inside the flow.
case.venc.achado2.t: Communication was the key to the delivery working
case.venc.achado2.d: Self-service existing was no use if the customer only found out about the problem after the charge failed. Alongside the flow came the proactive notice that the invoice was coming due, so they could move the date beforehand if they needed to.
case.venc.achado3.t: The flow had to be end to end
case.venc.achado3.d: From checking outstanding balances to simulating the new amount, through the rule-based blocks and paying off what was open. Stopping halfway would push the customer over to support.
case.venc.gal1.t: Every business rule made explicit in the flow
case.venc.img.fluxo: Flow of the self-service due date change, with the decisions and the message for each path
case.venc.cap.fluxo: The flow with the copy of every message already written. The three blocking conditions live in the path, not in support.
case.venc.gal2.t: How it looks in the app
case.venc.gal2.d: In 2025 this flow shipped as a chatbot with a decision tree. We have since rebuilt it on a new LLM tool with generative content.
case.venc.cap.menu: The entry point through the assistant, with topics organized by stage of the journey.
case.venc.cap.opcoes: Changing the due date sits with the other contract changes, in the same place.
case.venc.img.regras: The assistant's answer for someone without an active subscription
case.venc.cap.regras: The negative path is resolved there too: anyone without an active subscription gets the answer straight away.
case.venc.resultado.titulo: Solved alone, three times out of four.
case.venc.res1.n: Retention = the customer completes the change without falling through to a human. In the first weeks it was above 80%, and the level held once the novelty effect passed.
case.venc.res2.l: CSAT on the flow, above the support average at the time
case.venc.res2.n: Measured in the rating the assistant itself asks for when it closes the conversation.
case.venc.res3.l: between defining the scope, development, testing and deploy
case.venc.resultado.fecho1: Three out of four requests solved with no human support beat the target we had set, which was 50%. Customers who entered the flow landed in the right place and could use the tool in every scenario we had mapped.
case.venc.resultado.fecho2: From there, other self-service features for managing the subscription entered the roadmap, on the same logic of solving things before the contact happens.
case.cj.capa.sub: creating the practice and strengthening a client first culture
case.cj.meta.plataforma: The whole journey, end to end
case.cj.tldr.contexto: As the company grew, the customer's voice was partly left aside, and each area was following only its own slice of the journey.
case.cj.tldr.acao: We set up the practice, its objectives, method and metrics, and started bringing the customer's side consistently and directly into the forums where business decisions are made.
case.cj.tldr.resultado: In the first half the contact rate was already down 20%, and five new fronts entered the product roadmap through the studies the area ran.
case.cj.contexto.titulo: The customer journey was neither mapped nor monitored.
case.cj.contexto.p1: The company grew fast and customer culture became a secondary subject. Each area saw its own slice, and the symptom was decisions not being made, often for lack of information.
case.cj.contexto.p2: The area was born with a big challenge: how do you map an end-to-end journey that basically every area of the company intervenes in? And how do you get those areas to run the prioritized actions when you are a diagnosis team and not an execution one?
case.cj.quote1.t: Customer Journey does not replace the specialist areas. It organizes the problem and adds depth before it becomes a solution.
case.cj.quote1.a: The thesis that opened the kick-off of the practice
case.cj.discovery.metodo: The method had to produce knowledge for decisions, not just for reports. We set up a continuous cycle: listen to every channel, find where the friction costs the most, turn it into a hypothesis with a target metric and a success criterion, hand it to the area that owns the problem and follow the result alongside them.
case.cj.ct1.d: The diagnosis of the problem, the thesis that set the scope, the structure of the team and a 30, 60 and 90 day plan with a defined deliverable at each phase.
case.cj.ct2.d: Support, post-trip ratings, social media, store reviews and surveys read together for the first time, plus shadowing sessions as a customer and a benchmark against 14 mobility brands. Out of that came the ranking of friction by volume and criticality.
case.cj.ct3.d: Contact rate per booking as the primary metric and promoters in the post-trip rating as the secondary one, with a target negotiated through December. In the same move, we revisited an inherited NPS that had no valid sample.
case.cj.ct4.d: One study per theme, in the order the matrix pointed to: sign-up, billing, account blocking, fleet cleanliness, the support agent, and one real overdue-payment case reconstructed minute by minute. Each one with real conversations read, root cause analysis, a benchmark and testing with customers.
case.cj.ct5.d: The recap of the half fed into the product reprioritization for the year. Ten fronts came out of it, ordered by impact, with billing, sign-up and account blocking at the top, and five of them were new to the portfolio.
case.cj.achado1.t: Operational problems were the biggest detractors of experience
case.cj.achado1.d: What drags the rating down is not the app, it is the dirty car, the pickup that will not go through and the charge the customer does not understand. That changed the question the company was asking: instead of improving support, fix what generates the contact.
case.cj.achado2.t: A payment problem is not one problem
case.cj.achado2.d: What arrived labeled as billing had different root causes: a card that fails, an amount calculated wrong, an outstanding balance nobody can settle on their own, and the block that comes afterwards. Treated as a single theme, the volume was masking four problems with different owners and different fixes.
case.cj.achado3.t: Depth costs less than redoing everything
case.cj.achado3.d: Going deep on one theme at a time led to small, surgical changes with a big effect. Superficial mapping did the opposite: it pointed at the symptom across the whole journey and ended in a recommendation to refactor everything, which nobody prioritizes.

case.cj.resultado.titulo: The first results came in halfway through the cycle
case.cj.res1.n: First half of 2026 against the start of the year. The area's primary metric.
case.cj.res2.l: of promoters in the post-trip rating
case.cj.res2.n: Only the top score counts as a promoter. It hit the target in one month of the half and then fell back.
case.cj.res3.l: new fronts in the product roadmap because of the studies
case.cj.res3.n: They did not exist in the portfolio before. Each one with a defined owning area.
case.cj.resultado.p1: The number that holds up the others is the least showy one: loss of subscribers in their first three months fell by almost a quarter over the half, tracking closely with the drop in contacts per trip. But a good part of that gain still came from support efficiency rather than from a root cause actually solved, and it is exactly that difference between reducing contacts and reducing problems that set the queue for the next half.
